samples.text:
Advertisements are everywhere today, on television, on the internet and in the streets. Many of them try to make people believe that they need a product which they did not want before. This essay will explain how advertisers do this and whether it should be controlled.

Advertisers use different methods to persuade people. One common method is to use famous people like actors or footballers. When fans see their favourite star using a product, they want to buy it too because they want to be like him. Another method is to make people feel that their life is not good enough without the product. For example, a advert for a new phone shows happy young people with many friends, so the viewers think they will be more popular if they buy this phone. Also, advertisers use social media to collect information about users and show them ads which is based on their interests, so it is very hard to ignore them.

In my opinion, some control is necessary. Firstly, children are easily influenced by adverts and they often ask their parents to buy toys or unhealthy snacks. Governments should ban adverts for children in some times, for example during cartoons. Secondly, adverts should not give false information or promise things that the product can not do. However, I think adverts cannot be banned completely because companies need to tell people about their products and it help the economy.

In conclusion, advertisers create new wants by using celebrities, making people feel unhappy with their lives and targeting them online. I believe that governments should control adverts, especially for children, but not stop them totally.

samples.text:
Modern advertising frequently goes beyond informing consumers about products and instead convinces them that they need things they had never previously considered buying. This essay will explain the main techniques advertisers use to create such desires and argue that some regulation is justified.

One of the most effective strategies is to link a product with an attractive lifestyle or identity. Rather than focusing on what a car or a watch actually does, advertisements often show glamorous, successful people using it, suggesting that buyers will share that status. Advertisers also exploit people's insecurities. Beauty and fitness companies, for instance, may highlight minor imperfections that consumers had never worried about and then present their product as the solution. In addition, digital marketing has made persuasion more powerful than ever. By analysing people's browsing history, companies can target individuals with personalised adverts at exactly the moment they are most likely to make an impulse purchase, while social media influencers present sponsored products as if they were genuine personal recommendations.

I believe these practices should be controlled to some extent. The strongest case concerns children, who are less able to recognise persuasive intent, so advertising aimed at young audiences, particularly for unhealthy food and expensive toys, should be strictly limited. Transparency is also essential: influencers ought to be required to label paid content clearly, so that followers can distinguish advice from marketing. Furthermore, there should be clearer rules about how personal data can be used for targeting. That said, a total ban on persuasive advertising would be neither practical or desirable, as advertising funds much of the media and allows new businesses to reach customers.

In conclusion, advertisers create new wants by associating products with desirable lifestyles, exploiting insecurities and using personal data. Sensible regulation, especially to protect children and ensure transparency, would reduce the harmful effects without undermining legitimate marketing.
samples.why: Clear position with both questions answered and supported · well-organised paragraphs with clear central ideas · good range of vocabulary (exploit insecurities, impulse purchase) · frequent error-free sentences, one minor slip (neither ... or).

samples.text:
Much of modern advertising is not designed to meet existing demand but to manufacture it, persuading consumers that a product they had never heard of is suddenly indispensable. The techniques involved have become increasingly sophisticated, and in my view they warrant a degree of regulation, although not an outright ban.

At the core of most campaigns lies emotional association. Advertisers rarely sell objects on their practical merits; instead they sell the feelings and identities attached to them. A pair of trainers becomes a symbol of athletic success, while a luxury handbag is presented as evidence of sophistication. By repeatedly pairing a product with images of happiness, attractiveness or status, advertisers create a sense that ownership will deliver these qualities. A related tactic is the creation of dissatisfaction. Cosmetic and technology companies in particular are adept at convincing consumers that what they already own is inadequate, so that a perfectly functional phone begins to feel embarrassing the moment a new model is launched. Digital platforms have intensified these methods, allowing firms to target individuals with personalised messages and to reach them through influencers whose endorsements feel like the advice of a friend.

Some control over these practices seems reasonable. Children, who are especially susceptible to persuasion, deserve particular protection, and restrictions on advertising during children's programming or on apps aimed at them would be a sensible starting point. Clear disclosure rules for sponsored content would help adults recognise when they are being marketed to, and stricter limits on the collection of personal data would curb the most intrusive forms of targeting. However, advertising also finances free media and enables smaller companies to compete, so heavy-handed prohibition would do more harm than good.

In conclusion, advertisers generate new desires by attaching emotional meaning to products, fostering dissatisfaction and exploiting personal data. Targeted regulation, focusing on children, transparency and privacy, would limit manipulation while preserving the legitimate benefits of advertising.
samples.why: Both questions answered with a balanced, well-supported position · ideas logically sequenced and extended with apt examples · sophisticated, precise lexis (indispensable, susceptible, heavy-handed) · wide range of error-free structures.
